summary: A paper from IBM researchers on describing data so it can be shared across a network. They sort differences in how data is represented into three levels, starting with the very local, like character sets and number formats, and argue a data description language could help bridge them.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 242 proposes a language for describing the structure and representation of shared data. A data management system could use descriptions to transform data for a different computer.

questions: data description language for shared data
subtitle: A language proposal for describing shared data structures and representations.

tldr.problem: Computers represent individual values, collections and complex data structures differently, making shared data difficult to interpret and transform.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal describes data types and nested structures, with properties for names, locks, authorization, repetition, conditions and references.
tldr.outcome: A data management system could use source and target descriptions to transform data between representations.

today: RFC 242 is a data description proposal published in July 1971. The unit metadata lists its status as Unknown.

sections.title: Differences in Data Representation
sections.content:
The paper groups data representation differences into local value formats, the arrangement of collections, and complex structures such as indexed files or linked data. Networks make these differences more visible because data moves between systems.

The Network/440 approach is to describe the aspects of data that may need transformation. A data manager could use one description for the current representation and another for the desired copy.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers may encode values differently, organize collections differently and build complex structures differently. Descriptions can explain these differences so data can be transformed.

sections.title: Types and Grouped Structures
sections.content:
The language describes structure through groupings of data type codes. Machine-dependent codes include floating point, fixed point, character, complex, packed decimal and logical values. The machine-independent bit type can describe data that does not match the storage machine's native types; null and omit codes distinguish counted items without data from data to ignore.

Parentheses form nested groups, and the order of elements in a group specifies their order in the data collection.
sections.plainLanguage: Type codes say what each value represents, and parentheses show how values are grouped. A bit type can describe data even when a machine does not store that type directly.

sections.title: Properties and References
sections.content:
Descriptions can attach names, locking units and authorization codes to data items. Repetition and condition modifiers can repeat items or include them only when a condition is true. Named descriptions can be reused in another description.

The RFC also defines ways to select parts of a data set by moving down or up a structure, or forward or backward within a level. These operators support selecting named items and subsets by their contents.
sections.plainLanguage: Descriptions can name parts, mark access properties, repeat elements or make them conditional. They can also select particular parts of a nested data set.
